title: Clustering at scale: hierarchy, K-means, BFR, and CURE
summary: Use Lecture 3 as the canonical clustering source: choose a cluster geometry, calculate K-means updates, then scale the representation with BFR or CURE and evaluate it honestly.
objectives: Derive and calculate the K-means objective and updates
Explain BFR DS/CS/RS summaries and CURE representatives
Match evaluation metrics to labels and decisions

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture 3 defines the official clustering scope; Assignment 1 supplies the required hierarchical-clustering calculation. The provided MMDS package has no dedicated clustering chapter, so that textbook gap remains explicit.

sections.title: Choose geometry before algorithm
sections.body: Clustering is a partitioning decision over a representation and a similarity rule. Hierarchical methods make merge and stopping choices explicit; the result depends on whether closeness means a nearest pair, farthest pair, average distance, or a representative.

sections.title: K-means is an alternating objective
sections.body: K-means assigns each point to a representative and recomputes the representative. The two updates reduce the within-cluster squared-error objective, but initialization, the choice of $K$, and the metric can leave a locally optimal answer that is not the useful answer.

sections.title: Scale the summary, not the raw data
sections.body: BFR keeps sufficient statistics for confident discard-set clusters, compression-set summaries for uncertain groups, and a retained set for outliers. CURE keeps a few dispersed representatives and shrinks them toward the mean so a scalable summary preserves more shape than one centroid.

sections.title: Evaluate the decision you actually need
sections.body: Without labels, inspect cohesion, separation, and stability relative to the chosen geometry. With labels, purity is an external signal, not proof of utility; report its cluster-count sensitivity and connect the metric to the downstream decision.

math.name: K-means distortion
math.explanation: The distortion $J(R,Z)$ adds the squared distance from each point $x_i$ to the representative $z_{r(i)}$ of its assigned cluster.

math.name: BFR sufficient statistics
math.purpose: Summarize a cluster for later assignment without retaining every point.
math.explanation: BFR stores a count $N$, coordinate sums $\mathrm{SUM}$, and coordinate-wise squared sums $\mathrm{SUMSQ}$ so means and variances can be recovered for a compact cluster summary.

symbols.meaning: number of points in the summary

examples.title: K-means arithmetic checkpoint
steps: Choose the closest representative for every point.
Replace each representative with the mean of its assigned points.
Recompute the objective and record whether the loss decreased.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Merge clusters according to a defined distance between two clusters, then stop at the requested hierarchy level.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: The representation and distance are meaningful for the data, and the merge rule plus stopping condition are stated before comparing results.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: Single-link uses the minimum cross-cluster distance, complete-link the maximum, and average-link the mean; the smallest linkage score is merged next.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: For each pair of clusters, aggregate all cross-cluster distances with min, max, or mean, merge the best pair, and update the hierarchy.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: swapping single, complete, and average linkage; ignoring bridge points; or claiming a result without naming the distance and stopping rule.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Partition points into K clusters and choose representatives that minimize within-cluster squared error.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: K is fixed, the representative is a mean in the chosen geometry, and squared Euclidean error is an appropriate objective for the representation.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: With representatives fixed, nearest assignment does not increase loss; with assignments fixed, replacing each representative by its mean does not increase loss.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Alternate assignment and update steps while tracking $J(R,Z)=\sum_i\lVert x_i-z_{r(i)}\rVert^2$; stop when the state or objective stabilizes.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: treating monotonic loss as global optimality, forgetting initialization and K, or using a metric that disagrees with the cluster geometry.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Cluster data that does not fit in memory by retaining compact summaries instead of every point.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: A confident cluster can be summarized by sufficient statistics, uncertain groups can be compressed, and isolated points may need to remain explicit.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: BFR separates confident discard-set points (DS), uncertain compression-set groups (CS), and retained outliers (RS), without silently forcing uncertainty into DS.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Maintain $N$, $\mathrm{SUM}$, and $\mathrm{SUMSQ}$ for compact clusters, test new points against the summary, and delay or retain assignments when confidence is insufficient.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: putting every uncertain point in DS, losing RS outliers, or assuming summary statistics preserve arbitrary cluster shapes and boundaries.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Represent large clusters with a small set of points that preserves dispersed or non-spherical shape.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: Cluster shape matters, representative points can be selected across the cluster, and shrinking toward the mean is an acceptable noise reduction.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: Several dispersed representatives retain boundary and shape evidence while shrinkage pulls them toward the mean for a more stable compact representation.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: Select representative points across a cluster, move each toward the cluster mean by a shrinkage factor, and use the representatives for scalable comparison or assignment.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: replacing CURE with one centroid, forgetting shrinkage, or claiming shape preservation without stating the representative selection.

contrastDrills.pair: Single vs complete vs average linkage
contrastDrills.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three hierarchical linkage rules?
choices: Single uses the closest pair, complete the farthest pair, and average the mean pairwise distance
Single uses the mean, complete the closest pair, and average the farthest pair
All three use the same pair but stop at different cluster counts
Single is K-means, complete is BFR, and average is CURE
contrastDrills.explanation: Single-link uses the minimum cross-cluster distance, complete-link uses the maximum, and average-link uses the average of cross-cluster pair distances.
contrastDrills.misconception: Remembering the names without tying each rule to its aggregation over cross-cluster distances.
contrastDrills.repair: For every linkage, say min, max, or mean before judging which clusters merge.

criticalQuestions.prompt: When would you prefer CURE or BFR over plain K-means?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare shape preservation and memory constraints, then state the cost of the richer summary.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Use CURE when dispersed or non-spherical shape matters, BFR when the data is too large for memory and compact sufficient statistics are available, and K-means when the centroid geometry and objective are appropriate.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What evidence would make a high-purity clustering result unconvincing?
criticalQuestions.angle: Test the metric against cluster count, geometry, and the downstream decision.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Many tiny clusters, a mismatch between the similarity metric and the task, or no stability and downstream usefulness would weaken the purity claim.
